title: Mediator and Memento Patterns
summary: Two lower-frequency-but-real behavioral patterns: centralizing how objects talk to each other, and snapshotting an object's state for undo without breaking encapsulation.

slides.markdown:
Two patterns that solve unrelated problems but show up together in advanced interviews. **Mediator** stops a group of objects from all holding direct references to each other by routing their communication through one central hub — a chat room's `User` objects never talk directly, only through the `ChatRoom`. **Memento** lets you snapshot an object's internal state and restore it later — the mechanism behind undo — without exposing that internal state to whoever's holding the snapshot.

Both are less common in day-to-day code than Strategy or Observer, but both solve real, recognizable problems once you've seen the shape.

slides.sectionTitle: Mediator: centralize how objects talk to each other instead of a mesh of references
slides.markdown:
Picture a chat room with five `User` objects. If every user needs to send messages to every other user, the naive design has each `User` holding direct references to all four others — a **mesh** of connections that grows as `n²` with the number of users, and means adding a sixth user requires updating all five existing ones to know about it.

**Mediator** breaks the mesh: each `User` only holds a reference to one `ChatRoom` object, and sends messages through it — `chatRoom.send(message, fromUser)`. The `ChatRoom` (the mediator) is the only object that knows about every user, and it's responsible for routing the message to the right recipients.

Users become simpler and decoupled from each other; all the routing complexity moves into one well-defined place instead of being smeared across every participant.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: many-to-many object references replaced by a single mediator hub
slides.markdown:
Without Mediator, five objects that all need to talk to each other require up to ten direct connections (a full mesh). With Mediator, each object needs exactly one connection — to the mediator — and the mediator holds the connections to everyone.

![Side by side: five Users fully interconnected in a mesh vs. five Users each connected only to a central ChatRoom hub](assets/mediator-mesh-vs-hub.svg)

The total number of connections drops from roughly n² to n, and every user's code only ever needs to know about one type: the mediator's interface.

assets.alt: Side by side: five Users fully interconnected in a mesh vs. five Users each connected only to a central ChatRoom hub

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a chat-room Mediator routing messages between User objects
Pitfall: the mediator becoming a god object that knows too much
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Centralizing communication in a Mediator is strictly a win — the more logic I move into it, the more decoupled everything else becomes."

**Why it's wrong:** if `ChatRoom` grows to also handle message persistence, spam filtering, user permissions, and notification delivery, it's absorbed every responsibility the individual objects shed — the mesh of coupling didn't disappear, it just relocated into one enormous class that now knows and does everything. This **god object** becomes exactly as hard to change safely as the mesh was, just concentrated in a single file instead of scattered across several.

**Correct model:** a mediator should coordinate, not implement every concern itself — a `ChatRoom` should route messages, while persistence, spam filtering, and permissions live in their own collaborators the mediator calls out to. If the mediator's responsibility list keeps growing, that's the same signal a bloated class always gives, regardless of what pattern name is attached to it.

slides.sectionTitle: Memento: capture and restore an object's internal state without breaking encapsulation
slides.markdown:
Undo needs a way to save an object's exact internal state and restore it later. The naive approach — exposing every private field via getters so an external `HistoryManager` can read and later write them back — breaks encapsulation: now any code with access to those getters/setters can silently corrupt the object's internal invariants, not just the undo system.

**Memento** solves this by having the object itself (the **originator**) create an opaque snapshot object (the **memento**) containing everything needed to restore it — but only the originator can actually read the memento's contents back out. External code (the **caretaker**, like a `HistoryManager`) can store and pass mementos around, but never inspect or modify what's inside one.

The originator controls both what goes into a snapshot and how it's restored; the caretaker just manages *when* to keep or discard snapshots.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: originator, memento, and caretaker roles
slides.markdown:
The **originator** creates a memento from its own state and can restore itself from one. The **caretaker** holds a history of mementos but never opens them. Only the originator can read a memento's contents — the caretaker treats it as a sealed box.

![An Originator creating a Memento and handing it to a Caretaker, which stores it but cannot read its contents](assets/memento-roles.svg)

This is what keeps Memento from breaking encapsulation the way exposed getters/setters would: the caretaker manages *timing* (when to save, when to restore) without ever touching the actual internal data.

assets.alt: An Originator creating a Memento and handing it to a Caretaker, which stores it but cannot read its contents

slides.sectionTitle: Code: undo/redo for a text editor using Memento snapshots
Compare: Memento vs Command-based undo — snapshotting state vs replaying inverse actions
slides.markdown:
| | Memento-based undo | [Command](command-pattern)-based undo |
|---|---|---|
| What's stored | A full (or incremental) snapshot of state | The action taken, plus enough info to reverse it |
| Memory cost | Can be expensive for large state, snapshot per step | Usually cheap — an action object, not a full copy |
| Restoring | Just overwrite current state with the snapshot | Compute and apply the inverse of each action |
| Best fit | State is small, or hard to reverse via an inverse operation (e.g. a fully re-rendered document) | Actions have a natural, cheap-to-compute inverse (undo an insert by deleting) |

**How to decide:** if reversing an action is easy to express as "do the opposite" (Command's approach), that's usually cheaper. If the state is small or an inverse operation isn't naturally definable, snapshotting with Memento is simpler even if less memory-efficient.
